#6200. Singapore Airlines Reconsiders New Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-new cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change…

On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the new business class seat design.

In response to this, he reportedly said “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin said this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the new design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”

To state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a new business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

Is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a new business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#6198. Amex Business Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 300K Points Welcome Offer

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express is one of the most perks-rich business cards out there, and is useful if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 300,000 points are worth a staggering $5,100. As I see it, that’s basically the best welcome offer you’ll find on any card.

Let me emphasize that Amex uses a variety of factors when deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Platinum Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible Amex Business Platinum bonus through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there.

That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method. However, it can always be worth checking back every so often, because the promotions people are targeted for can change over time.

The Amex Business Platinum bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to nearly $6,700 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners. Also keep in mind that having this card lets you unlock the full value of Amex Pay With Points, potentially allowing you to get up to 1.54 cents of value per point toward the cost of airfare on a designated airline (this comes in the form of a 35% Pay with Points rebate, up to one million points per year). You could then use that redemption rate for all your linked Amex Membership Rewards cards.

Just to give a couple of examples of how much value those 300,000 Membership Rewards points could get you:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find the Amex Business Platinum to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Platinum, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). While this isn’t the most rewarding card in terms of the return on spending, it does have a huge number of valuable perks, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the Amex Business Platinum annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

Just to give a sense of the immense value, below is a basic rundown of the Amex Business Platinum credits, which should for many people help offset the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

Of particular note is that the card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits, in the form of a $300 credit semi-annually, and largely helps with offsetting the annual fee. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

When it comes to the Amex Business Platinum rewards structure, the card offers:

There’s another incentive to put at least $250,000 in eligible purchases on the card each calendar year, as that unlocks the following credits, which can be worth up to $3,600:

Read a full review of the Amex Business Platinum Card here.

There’s currently an excellent Amex Business Platinum Card bonus, which is as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points upon completing minimum spending. While the spending requirement is significant, so is the number of points you can earn, so this is worth it if you’re eligible, and can swing it.

This card offers all kinds of great perks that can help offset the annual fee, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status, and more. You can even see what offer you’re eligible for on the card without a hard credit pull, so it’s worth seeing if you qualify, in my opinion.

Do you plan on picking up the Amex Business Platinum Card? What kind of a welcome offer are you eligible for?

#6197. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

Every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only showed up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):

So this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

It’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

American had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

What do you make of this American pilot being arrested?

#6194. Buy Etihad Guest Miles With 60% Bonus (2.0 Cents Each): Worth It?

Etihad Guest has just launched its latest promotion on buying miles, which is being marketed as the biggest offer of the year. With this, members can buy Etihad miles with a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire them for as little as two cents each.

Is that offer worth it? Let’s cover all the details, but I’ll say right away that I think this offer has fairly limited appeal, and you should only take advantage of this with a specific use in mind.

Link: Buy Etihad Guest miles with a bonus

Between 12:01AM GST on November 12 and 11:59PM GST on November 22, 2026, Etihad Guest is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger bonus the more miles you buy, as follows:

Note that purchased Etihad Guest miles post within 72 hours of completing the purchase (typically faster than that), and that purchased miles don’t count toward Etihad Guest elite status.

Etihad Guest ordinarily charges 3.2 cents per purchased mile, and there are no further taxes and fees. That’s before any bonuses or discount. With the 60% bonus, if you maxed out this promotion you’d receive a total of 320,000 Etihad Guest miles at a cost of $6,400, which is a rate of two cents per Etihad Guest mile.

Etihad Guest limits members to purchasing 200,000 miles per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. The exception is Etihad Guest Platinum members, who can purchase up to 300,000 miles per year, before any bonuses.

The current Etihad Guest buy miles promotion is described as the biggest offer of the year. To compare this to other offers we’ve seen so far this year, we’ve seen bonuses of 25-50% (2.56 cents to 2.13 cents per mile), as well as discounts of up to 35% (2.08 cents per mile).

As you can see, Etihad Guest’s current offer gives you the best cost per mile so far this year. However, Etihad isn’t exactly aggressive with selling miles, so it’s hard to get too excited about any of these amounts.

Etihad Guest mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There are lots of ways to redeem Etihad Guest miles. While the airline doesn’t belong to one of the major alliances, there are many ways to redeem the miles on both Etihad and on partner airlines.

Below you can find the award chart for travel exclusively on Etihad. The pricing is based on the one-way distance of travel. Note that these redemption rates are specifically for situations where there’s GuestSeat availability, which is Etihad’s capacity controlled, saver award space.

If you see higher award pricing than what’s listed below, that generally means there’s not saver award space, and redemptions won’t be a very good deal. Furthermore, in some situations you’ll find higher saver level award costs, including for travel in the carrier’s A380 first class.

Etihad Guest has a separate award chart for travel on partner airlines, which is also distance based, and you can find that below. This is based on the one-way distance, and you can’t mix airline partners on a single award.

The main reason to consider collecting Etihad Guest miles is because the program has access to a lot more Etihad award space than partner programs do. Partner programs, like American AAdvantage and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, typically only have access to a subset of premium cabin Etihad availability. Furthermore, if you want to fly in Etihad’s The Residence, your ticket needs to be issued by Etihad, so an Etihad Guest award redemption would qualify.

There are two major catches when it comes to Etihad Guest, in addition to not really having slam dunk redemption values:

I’d really only recommend buying Etihad Guest miles with a very specific use in mind, if you know what you’re doing.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Etihad Guest miles to be worth 1.1 cents each. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Etihad Guest miles than that.

Etihad Guest miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Note that you can only reset the expiration of your miles by crediting a flight to the program every 18 months, so other activity wouldn’t help in that regard.

Keep in mind that there are many ways to earn Etihad Guest miles, so outright buying miles isn’t the only option. Etihad Guest also partners with select transferable points currencies. In the United States, you can move points to Etihad Guest at a 1:1 ratio from Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so that gives you quite a bit of flexibility.

Admittedly not everyone has access to credit cards in the United States, and some people may also prefer to just buy miles if they can acquire them at a reasonable cost.

Etihad Guest is selling miles with up to a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy miles for as little as two cents each. This could be worth it if you have a specific use in mind, but Etihad Guest just seems rather unserious with its buy miles promotions, since the program isn’t that lucrative, in terms of redemption rates, and the policies for changing and canceling awards is also incredibly frustrating.

So for a vast majority of people, I’d recommend giving this offer a pass, unless you’ve done the math, and it checks out.

Does anyone plan on buying Etihad Guest miles with this offer?

#6192. World Of Hyatt Brand Explorer: Free Night Awards For Staying At New Brands

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night award awards. In this post, I’d like to talk about one of the often overlooked ways to earn Hyatt free nights, which is with World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion.

This offers World of Hyatt members the opportunity to earn free night awards for exploring Hyatt’s portfolio. Given the huge brand inflation that Hyatt has seen in recent years, this can potentially offer up to seven free night awards, and counting.

With World of Hyatt’s Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a Category 1-4 free night certificate for every five unique Hyatt brands you stay at. When it comes to earning Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

If you want to see how many Hyatt brands you’ve stayed at, you can do so either through the World of Hyatt website or mobile app. Just go to the “Brand Explorer” section, and there will be a display showing how many unique brands you’ve stayed at (including which ones), and also how many free night certificates you’ve earned.

When it comes to redeeming Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

Of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt currently has 38 brands, which are as follows:

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

Air Canada's chief operations officer, Mark Nasr, used the Skift Aviation Forum in New York to argue the carrier was the first premium airline in North America — citing lie-flat seats, all-aisle access, and investments in concierge services and food and beverage — and said the missing piece now is reliability. Nasr said Air Canada's on-time performance sits in the mid-70s and should be in the low 80s, which he said would make it best of breed in North America. He pointed to staffing levels, more training, more decision-making freedom for employees, and schedules with enough buffer for weather and airport construction as the levers. After what Nasr called the largest snowstorm in Toronto's recorded history in January, the airline started making cancellation decisions earlier and now aims to rebook customers from the point of origin rather than at the hub. Air Canada also rolled out its first large-scale AI agent tool to all contact center staff, which Nasr said is meant to improve service without adding cost rather than cut front-line jobs. Nasr, who spent nearly a decade in the carrier's loyalty business, said loyalty is a multiplier on a base, and that the program can't do its full job if the base is weak.

#6189. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

#6188. California City Approves Protections for Polyamorous Arrangements

Nobody could have seen this coming, except all the conservatives who said it would happen.

Then-mayor of West Hollywood Chelsea Lee Byers attends the Stonewall Democratic Club’s 50th-anniversary celebration in West Hollywood, Calif., November 15, 2025.

Wilbert Roberts/Getty Images for Connor Treacy

The West Hollywood City Council unanimously approved an ordinance that allows multi-partner relationships (like a so-called throuple) to formally register as a domestic relationship and receive certain legal protections at the local level, such as visitation rights in jail and rental privileges. A “multi-partner relationship,” per the ordinance, requires that the individuals involved share “the common necessities of life,” are over age 18, are competent enough to enter a contract, are all participating consensually, are “responsible for one another’s welfare,” and are not related by blood or a member of an already declared partnership. There is no expressed limit to the number of individuals who may be involved in a recognized multi-partner relationship, and people living outside the city can register their relationship.

The idea of protections for polyamory was brought to Councilmember Chelsea Lee Byers last year by Christina Fialho, an attorney who founded the “Rewrite the BiLine” organization that “reshape[s] cultural norms and drive[s] policy change” through media narratives to “advance health equity, economic opportunity, and civil rights for bi+ people and non-nuclear families.” Fialho told the Los Angeles Times that “this law is just the beginning. . . . I think it makes it possible for people to dream about a future they once thought was out of reach.” According to public records, the city council deemed it “necessary” to recognize “diverse relationship structures,” such as those involving more than two adults, because they are “becoming increasingly common.” The city frames the ordinance as an anti-discrimination measure with symbolic value:

#6185. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

The reason to get the aircraft on the ground before water finds its way into the avionics is well-established. The NTSB concluded that a Delta Boeing 767 investigation faced freezing flight control components as a result of leaking water that froze, limiting control over the aircraft’s ailerons. Here, the Frontier aircraft landed safely.

I covered a Delta flight in June where passengers were told to hold their bags in their laps for landing as water spread through the cabin approaching San Francisco. And the closest comparison is an Alaska Airlines flight from Honolulu to Anchorage that turned around after a sink overflow. Passengers reported two to four inches of standing water. Flight attendants tried to soak it up with paper towels. And some of you still walk into airplane lavatories barefoot.

#6180. Scoop: Frontier Airlines Plans First Class Service—Not Just Bigger Seats

Frontier Airlines is planning more than a bigger seat for first class. A new memo tells flight attendants that first class service standards are coming for flights beginning March 5, 2027, the same day its new front cabin launches. This follows my original scoop, since confirmed by the airline, that Frontier’s first class rolls out March 5, 2027. Under “Onboard service,” the airline now says: Our standard onboard services apply through March 4, 2027. New First Class service standards will be released for flights on and after March 5, 2027. This is a move toward a real first class service, and away from the Spirit Airlines ‘Big Front Seat’ approach to just selling more space. This hasn’t been announced publicly yet. The airline’s first class frequently asked questions, updated just yesterday, still says food and beverages are available for purchase. Specific standards are still to come. Frontier Has Confirmed The March 5 Launch Frontier originally announced first class in December 2024 for late 2025. Last month I reported that aircraft conversions were beginning, with the bigger seats sold as UpFront Plus during the transition. So getting the seat before the March 5 official launch doesn’t mean getting new service with it. Frontier publicly announced first class reservations on November 10, confirming March 5 travel and targeting that date for completion of the seating conversion: Eight first class seats: two rows in a 2-by-2 configuration, with up to 37 inches of pitch. More extra legroom: rows three through eight will offer up to 34 inches of pitch. UpFront Plus, with its blocked middle seat, continues in select rows. A First bundle advertised from $129 one way: first class seating, a carry-on, two checked bags and priority boarding. A Premium bundle advertised from $90 one way: extra legroom seating, a carry-on and priority boarding. The introductory offer requires buying the flight and bundle together by November 16, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. And these seats still don’t recline. Frontier describes them as “pre-reclined,” which means you can’t adjust the seatback. Power And Wi-Fi Are Coming Frontier now says USB-C charging will be offered in the first eight rows, not throughout the full coach cabin. Both power and Starlink wi-fi will roll out during 2027. Frontier’s new renderings show the charging setup: I’ve said that the lack of inflight internet has kept me from flying Frontier. Giving up hours of work can make the cheapest ticket actually more expensive. A bigger seat, power and working wi-fi make a big difference in my willingness to buy travel from them. Their operational reliability, however, is still a caution. Including drinks and food makes sense as it tries to have a product customers interested in a better experience will buy. They’ve had largely the cheap offerings but not the revenue opportunities from further upsells. It’s still not clear what the service standards will mean or translate into in the cabin. Unfortunately, for bookings made starting January 1, 2027, elite frequent flyers will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades to first class if they buy a bundle. And top tier Diamonds only qualify 24 hours prior to departure (18 for Platinum, 8 for Gold, and 4 for Silver). #6179. Not All Property Tax Cuts Are Created Equal

Fiscal conservatives’ aim should be the same as for other taxes: broaden the base, reduce the rate.

An aerial view of a suburban neighborhood in central Florida.

We can at least say this of last Tuesday: It was a great day for homeowners upset over their property taxes. Across five states, voters approved seven ballot measures to directly reduce or otherwise limit local taxes on different kinds of property. Conservatives, instinctively anti-tax in almost every instance, cheered these initiatives.

Yet nuance is needed. Given that taxation is the necessary price of government, conservatives have long accepted that some taxes are better than others. Likewise, some kinds of property taxes are preferable to others, and therefore, not all cuts to property taxes are created equal. Some may even be worse than the status quo.

John R. Puri is the Thomas L. Rhodes Fellow at National Review.

#6178. 6 Reasons Why Citi Strata Elite Beats Amex Platinum And Sapphire Reserve

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Citi Strata Elite earns 50% more points on unbonused spending than Amex Platinum or Chase Sapphire Reserve, and those points can become American Airlines miles. It also costs $200 – $300 less per year.

I’ve written a lot about the card’s enormous first-year value. But the more I’ve used the hotel benefit, the more I think there’s a case for the Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) beyond the initial bonus. Here are six things it does better than Amex Platinum and Sapphire Reserve – both excellent cards and I have them both.

Banks advertise how many transfer partners they have. A long list can include many I even actively avoid (Aeromexico, Thai Airways). Most banks are also limited in whom they can work with because major airline and hotel cobrand card agreements usually include exclusivity provisions that limit what competing banks can offer. American Express has Delta. Chase has United. Citi has American. Of those three, I’d take American AAdvantage. Strata Elite points transfer to American at 1:1. And American still offers some terrific partner redemptions. However, some of my best American redemptions are just regular domestic coach trips. I’ve written about getting 4 cents and even 8 cents per mile from economy awards. American will sometimes make a flight cheap in miles while keeping the cash fare high. You don’t need to want a first class suite halfway around the world to get value from this program. Citi still has international partners I want, including Air France KLM Flying Blue, Singapore Airlines and Qatar Airways. Chase’s Hyatt transfers are a real advantage on the hotel side. (I still wish Bank of America had its own transferable points program, with Alaska’s Atmos Rewards as a partner.) 2. The Hotel Credit Works Beyond A Short List Of Luxury Properties Strata Elite offers up to $300 off prepaid hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Citi Travel each calendar year. The discount comes off when you book, and applies to the room cost before taxes and fees. You can use it at ordinary hotels and independent properties, without restricting yourself to a luxury collection. Amex Platinum’s $600 annual hotel credit is split into two $300 periods and requires Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. Sapphire Reserve’s $500 The Edit credit is limited to that collection, with a maximum of $250 per qualifying booking. Chase also has an additional 2026 hotel credit, but that one is restricted to selected brands. Those programs can provide real value through breakfast, property credits and hotel loyalty benefits. Citi’s advantage is the much broader choice of hotels where I can use the discount. And I haven’t found that using Citi’s credit requires giving back the savings through a higher room rate. In January, I compared the Marriott at LaGuardia Airport: Citi Travel was $156 before taxes, while Marriott’s own member rate was $176. That’s $20 less per night before applying the credit. I still compare the room and cancellation terms, but Citi Travel has been competitive or even cheaper. I’ve also had little difficulty getting Marriott hotels to add my Bonvoy number at check-in and honor on-property benefits. Earlier this year I used the Strata Elite credit at a Marriott and received club lounge access. I similarly had no problem getting status recognition on a bank portal booking at a Westin this month. These third-party bookings generally aren’t supposed to be eligible for hotel points, elite-night credit or elite benefits. 3. It’s A Better Card For Everyday Spending Strata Elite earns 1.5 points per dollar on spending outside its bonus categories. Sapphire Reserve and Amex Platinum earn just one. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. #6176. IAG Launches Media Business to Cash In on Connected Passengers: Exclusive

Start your subscription today and be the first to all travel industry scoops.

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: IAG Media joins IAG Loyalty as a capital-light revenue driver for the European aviation group. IAG

Free Wi-Fi is anything but free for airlines. IAG now has to turn that bill into advertising revenue without annoying the people paying the fares.

International Airlines Group (IAG) is launching a standalone media and advertising business as it looks to turn its huge investment in Starlink Wi-Fi into a revenue opportunity.

The new company, IAG Media, will allow advertisers to reach the group's 122 million annual passengers through targeted campaigns, including personalized advertising on Starlink login portals and inflight entertainment systems.

Speaking exclusively to Skift, IAG Media CEO Nacho Tovar and Josh Peckham, chief commercial officer, outlined plans to transform how advertising is delivered onboard aircraft, using high-speed connectivity to move beyond the same commercials being shown to every passenger.

"Previously you got on board an aircraft... you were in this black box of no connectivity," explained Peckham. "Connectivity is the real driver of us being able to create that fully personalized experience."

Tovar said the technology would help IAG build what he descri

Tags: airlines, iag, jet stream, passenger experience, skift exclusive, skift intelligence, starlink, united airlines

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

International Airlines Group is launching IAG Media, a standalone U.K. company that will sell advertising against the group's 122 million annual passengers across British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus, Vueling, and LEVEL. The venture is tied to IAG's Starlink rollout, with half the fleet expected to be equipped by the end of 2026 as part of a program covering more than 500 aircraft. IAG Media CEO Nacho Tovar and Chief Commercial Officer Josh Peckham told Skift that connectivity allows advertising to be tailored by destination, cabin class, and customer profile, replacing a model in which every passenger sees the same adverts. The business spans two divisions — a products and platform arm building ad technology through connectivity, inflight entertainment, and AI, and an agency arm handling sales, campaigns, and creative — and plans personalized advertising across websites, apps, and PDF boarding passes, plus an audience extension product that reaches travelers on third-party platforms. Starlink is free for eligible IAG passengers, but industry estimates put installation costs at $300,000 to $500,000 per aircraft plus recurring fees, which frames the revenue question. IAG is not first: United launched Kinective Media in 2024, and Lufthansa Group has been developing its own media proposition. Tovar and Peckham declined to provide revenue forecasts or profitability targets, and both said a bad customer experience would damage the brands and the business.

#6174. Breeze’s David Neeleman: Chasing Old-School Metrics ‘Got Spirit to Die’

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Breeze Airways CEO David Neeleman at Skift Aviation Forum in New York City on November 12, 2026. Skift

While rivals battle the majors for the same travelers, Breeze has turned profitable by creating its own demand. Now it wants a cut of what those travelers spend on the ground.

Smaller airlines get into trouble when they try to compete with the majors, Breeze Airways founder and CEO David Neeleman said Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum.

Breeze has tried to stay out of their way, and Neeleman said the airline has posted four consecutive profitable quarters, with a fifth expected. The airline is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results.

Spirit, which shut down in May, shows the risk. As the carrier moved to bigger planes, it was pushed into the same markets as the Big Four. The majors then moved to bigger planes too, adding seats that cost them “less than half” what Spirit paid per seat, he said.

Skift Research has previously reported that U.S. low-cost carriers are stuck in oversupplied domestic leisure markets that pit them head-to-head with the

Tags: breeze airways, david neeleman, saf2026, skift aviation forum 2026, skift intelligence, ultra low-cost carriers

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Breeze Airways founder and CEO David Neeleman used the Skift Aviation Forum to argue that smaller U.S. carriers lose when they fly head-to-head with the Big Four, and that Breeze has avoided that fight by flying routes the majors skip. He said Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, though the airline is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results. Neeleman pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it ended up in the same markets as the majors, who added seats at a cost he said was "less than half" what Spirit paid per seat. Breeze instead manages to trip costs rather than CASM, sells a heavily premium cabin — about 41% of seats, soon 45% — and was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, according to Skift Research. Neeleman said AI has let Breeze slow hiring rather than cut staff, with three or four people in yield management overseeing 300 daily flights. He also wants Breeze to earn a cut of the economic activity its routes create in small markets, citing second-home buying in places like Vero Beach, Florida, and describing a Priceline-style commission model with first steps expected next year.

#6173. The Rise of the Rosé States

A rosé state’s political disposition is recognizably Republican, but that disposition is conditional on a normie GOP.

Karno Muji Saputra/Getty Images, NR Illustration

When Ted Cruz was up for reelection in Texas in 2024 (and Trump hadn’t yet been swept back into power), I had a conversation with a political operative who had just gotten back from running a mock debate with him. We talked about Cruz and John Cornyn and what kind of Republican each was, and how they would fare in a world where Trump completed his comeback.

I spitballed an idea that had been kicking around in my head for a time: that Texas wasn’t as red as everybody thought, or at least not as uniformly MAGA; that it was still much closer to the state George W. Bush took over from outgoing Governor Ann Richards in 1995; and that election results had largely masked an underlying political disposition that was a quite light shade of red. Given that reality, I said, Cornyn was a better indication of where Texas voters were than Cruz.

Karno Muji Saputra/Getty Images, NR Illustration

Daniel Foster is a contributing editor at National Review.

Korean Air is adding a second New York-area gateway.

The SkyTeam Alliance carrier will land at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) with flights from Seoul’s Incheon Airport (ICN) in May 2027, Korean Air said on Thursday. The new route to east of the Hudson River complements its long-standing twice-daily service to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Korean Air will offer daily flights to EWR from May 22. It will fly a Boeing 777-300ER on the route.

The airline did not say what 777 configuration it will fly to EWR. It flies planes with several layouts, including an older configuration with eight first class suites.

United Airlines launched its first-ever nonstop from EWR to ICN in September. The Star Alliance carrier flies a Boeing 787-9 on the route.

Korean Air’s new EWR flight comes at a time of change for the airline as it wraps up a merger with fellow Korean carrier Asiana. Korean will complete the customer-facing integration of Asiana on Dec. 17, a combination that will significantly increase its market share at ICN.

While the merger does not add any new U.S. destinations to Korean Air’s map, it does increase its presence at JFK to up to four daily flights including Asiana, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

First look: Inside Korean Air’s stunning new flagship lounge at LAX

Future schedules show Korean Air continuing to serve JFK with four daily flights through June 2027.

The new EWR flight will complement Korean Air’s JFK services and create a new connection with joint venture partner Delta Air Lines. The carriers have expanded their transpacific options in recent years with new routes, including Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) to ICN on Delta.

The partnership allows Delta and Korean Air to coordinate commercial matters, including fares and schedules, between the U.S. and South Korea.

Korean Air highlighted the expanded flight options and New Jersey’s pharmaceutical, biotechnology, financial, and logistics industrial clusters for its new EWR route.

EWR is Korean Air’s first new U.S. destinations since it added Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) in 2019.

#6170. U.S. Pilot Arrested At London Heathrow Airport, Admits Cocaine Possession—Passengers Owed Over $150,000 Compensation

A 64-year-old U.S. pilot arrested at London Heathrow has pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. Wayne Sigler, from Louisiana, was remanded in custody and faces two additional charges involving alleged drunkenness or unfitness for duty. According to the BBC’s report of information confirmed by the Metropolitan Police, Sigler was arrested on Sunday, November 1. He appeared in court on Saturday, November 7, and pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. His next hearing is scheduled for December 7 at Isleworth Crown Court. Those charges fall under the Railways and Transport Safety Act 2003. The law also covers preparing to fly, duties after reporting for work, and standby. The charges don’t establish that he flew passengers while impaired. Reporting on the incident doesn’t identify the airline or flight, and I can’t directly confirm this is the right individual but there’s a Wayne Sigler who identifies as an American Airlines pilot in federal campaign donation records, and online discussion pegs him as an American pilot who came to the airline via America West and US Airways. On November 1, American Airlines 39 to Miami and American AIrlines 91 to Chicago O’Hare were both cancelled, and American 85 to O’Hare departed nearly 5 hours late. What Delayed Passengers Are Owed A flight departing Heathrow is covered by U.K. passenger compensation rules regardless of where the airline is based. For a journey over 3,500 kilometers, such as London to the U.S., a qualifying arrival delay of more than four hours means £520 per person (~ US$690.42). A three-to-four-hour delay falls into the £260 band. An airline can avoid the compensation payment when extraordinary circumstances caused the disruption. But the U.K. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Lipton v BA Cityflyer rejected that defense in the case of a pilot’s illness. And paragraph 170 specifically addresses a pilot who drinks enough to be unfit to report for work. If that causes a cancellation, the court says the reason is “inherent in the airline’s activity and operations.” A plane with 250 passengers at £520 each would mean £130,000 in compensation or $172,500. There was a British Airways pilot who bragged about using cocaine during a Johannesburg layover. A flight attendant reported his messages, he was kept from operating the return flight, and the airline fired him. #6167. Rail To The Austin Airport Is Back On The Table—After Costs Soared And A Voter Bait-and-Switch

Austin’s airport used to be super convenient but it’s outgrown itself. There are just too many passengers for the size of the facility, at peak times it can be nearly body to body as you navigate through the terminal. What was once curb-to-gate in minutes, security wait times on peak travel days can be quite long. And traffic gets backed up heading into and out of the airport. There’s a long trek across the road and through a parking garage, up and down levels, to get to Uber or taxis. They’re building a new terminal and a new headhouse. The airport’s solution is to get (a lot) bigger. It will never recapture the ease of a smaller airport, and it’s going to mean more walking and showing up even earlier. One thing Austin doesn’t have is rail to the airport. Voters approved higher property taxes in 2020 to pay for it, but the cost of the project ballooned and train ambitions remained – but the airport connection got axed to save money. Now the mayor wants to start the process of planning again for a train to the airport. The much smaller light rail system now being developed will cost nearly double what was once estimated, even though it won’t reach the airport when it’s supposed to open in 2033. But since the airport is building an entirely new face to the facility, it makes sense to plan for how a train would approach and where the station would go. Plus, they’re going to be looking to have the airport pay for a portion of it. That’s part of what the mayor means when he talks about rail reaching the airport without new tax money. Mayor Kirk Watson lays out a three-mile extension of the planned train, mostly elevated, with a station at the airport. He says the Federal Transit Administration has agreed to a streamlined environmental review, and the next nine to twelve months will be spent working through costs and funding. His challenge is to deliver it “within our existing budget approved by voters – no new taxpayer dollars.” Latest #WatsonWire: It’s time to start the process to get rail to the airport. For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past. We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it. The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come. As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city. A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel. We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA. An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact. Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1. In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps. We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed. With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport. Read more: https://t.co/JTYqnnRyEE — Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026 Airport Rail Was Part Of What Voters Were Sold Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for.
