For years, our Austin Bergstrom International Airport (ABIA or AUS) operated beyond the capacity it was originally designed to accommodate. That’s a sign of success, and a reminder that we can’t build Austin’s future relying on infrastructure designed for its past.

We need to envision a successful future and prepare for it.

The “Journey With AUS” expansion project is delivering significant improvements in building the kind of airport a growing, globally connected city like Austin needs for decades to come.

As we build a better airport, we also need to think about how we’re going to get people there to catch their flights and how to get them out of there to participate in our city.

A world-class airport needs a multimodal, world-class transportation system to connect to it. Sure, we need to improve roadway access. And we also should give people more choices about how they travel.

We need to have the same long-term vision for Austin light rail that we’ve had for ABIA.

An airport rail connection has been part of Austin’s long-term transportation vision for years. With Journey with AUS, we have a chance to plan these projects strategically rather than trying to connect them after the fact.

Until now, Austin Transit Partnership (ATP) has appropriately prioritized navigating the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) process for phase 1 of our system. This year, ATP received the important Record of Decision (ROD) from FTA and completed, in record time, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for phase 1.

In addition to getting the ROD and completing the NEPA process, I’ve wanted all major design and construction contracts in place and assurance that all of our financial decision-making is guided by a financial stewardship protocol before ATP takes any other big next steps.

We have the ROD, the NEPA process is complete, the major contracts are in place, and the financial stewardship protocol is being followed.

With these important milestones met, we can now take a major step: ATP will start the planning activities for a potential extension to take Austin light rail all the way to the airport.

— Mayor Kirk Watson (@KirkPWatson) November 10, 2026

Austin rejected rail proposals in 2000 and 2014. The successful 2020 vote for a $7.1 billion project came when voters were home during the pandemic and governments were spending unprecedented sums on Covid relief. The city’s election explainer lays out a Blue Line running through downtown to the airport, an Orange Line connecting north and south Austin, and a downtown tunnel. There were also commuter rail and bus improvements, plus $300 million for housing intended to ‘prevent displacement’ along the transit corridors. The ballot itself pitched airport rail. Voters approved an additional 8.75 cents per $100 of taxable property value, described as $437.50 a year on a home with $500,000 of taxable value, with federal funding expected to cover about 45% of the cost. Then the rail cost estimate exploded. By 2022, the original rail component had gone from $5.8 billion to $10.3 billion. That was blamed on inflation, land costs and construction costs but it was also the result of design changes to add more undeground tunneling. Without enough money, the connection out to the airport was dropped. The train got chopped from 20 miles to 9.8 miles. 26 stations down to 15 It lost airport servic and a downtown subway And the cost went from $5.8 billion to $8.2 billion With opening delayed from a planned 2029 reaching the airport to 2033 without it. The airport got dropped from ‘phase one’ and became labeled a ‘preferred priority extension’ if additional funding materialized. Now The Idea Is To Have The Airport Pay For Part Of It The Mayor repeatedly connects the rail extension to the airport’s ‘Journey With AUS’ expansion program. Austin is rebuilding its terminal frontage, roads and parking arrangements. And it’s building a new concourse. This is when you want to reserve space for a rail station. Journey With AUS uses airport revenues, airport revenue bonds, passenger facility charges and federal aviation grants. The airport sold $1.18 billion in May and plans $4.2 billion more through 2030. That money is spoken for, but the city owns the airport and it generates tremendous revenue. There are limits on what it can do with the money – the federal government makes grants and doesn’t want that money diverted. However, In 2021, the FAA began allowing on-airport rail infrastructure to receive airport funding even when the broader line serves people who aren’t using the airport. And 2025 FAA guidance says airports can contribute to ground access projects, including facilities beyond airport the property, provided airport funds support the airport-related share. So the airport link can open up airport funds now, as well as avoiding duplicate construction. The mayor frames the effort as “no new taxpayer dollars” but that’s different from “no new airport dollars” and the airport is owned by taxpayers. The Rail System’s Financing May Be Illegal, But The Election Could Change That The city created a separate public nonprofit corporation to pay for the train, so that the city itself wouldn’t be the one incurring debt. Then it held an election about the property tax rate, instead of one authorizing the city to borrow a specified amount of money. The city collects the property taxes and transfers the money to the special corporation which issues and pays interest on the bonds. Normally, in Texas, the city would have to specify an amount of debt to raise. If they later wanted to take on more debt, they’d have to go back to voters. Instead, they raised taxes by a specified amount and dedicated that tax stream to the project. Basically the city isn’t issuing the bonds, and isn’t taking on debt. The city also says it transfers the money each year, but future city councils could just stop making the transfers (winky, winky). There’s no city debt so they didn’t have to follow state rules for the city issuing debt. So property taxes support the borrowing, but the city isn’t mkaing a binding multiyear promise. There’s no debt. The state’s attorney general said this was completely illegal and sued. But he ran for Senate. After being impeached for corruption. This is the guy who spent the nation’s 250th birthday outside the country on vacation with the girlfriend he cheated on his wife (a state senator!) with. And he was videotaped partying in Dubai with fugitives. So he lost, along with every other Republican running for statewide office. It’s unclear whether the new attorney general will drop the case. For now, whether the state can take a tax increase and use it in perpetuity for a project that has ever-increasing capital costs, and then pivot later to use the funds to subsidize operations, remains tied up in the courts. There’s also a citizen lawsuit over the project’s bait and switch. Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for. Back in 2016 when I first started traveling to Austin frequently, the airport was one of the easier destinations to get in and out of. Then they moved Uber and Lyft to the remote parking lot 4 city blocks from the terminal doors and causing you to have drag your baggage upstairs, or downstairs to get to the pickup area depending on what level you exited the terminal. Not very convenient at all, and now, it has become very congested at times and all of the eating establishments and concessions are basically overrun at lunch, dinner, and breakfast. I hope they do the rebuild right.

The fundamental problem with light-rail systems is simple: How do people get from their homes to a rail stop?

If they have to drive (and park) there, they may as well just drive the rest of the way to their destination.

“ Voters agreed to the taxes for a project that was completely different than the one that the taxes are actually paying for.”

It’s quite common that driving & parking at a rail station then taking the train is far faster & cheaper than driving & parking at a major destination (such as an airport).

Voters never learn that transit systems always cost several times the original estimates while delivering less than promised. Austin’s results are nevertheless better than LAX’s people mover, let alone California’s high speed rail money pit. I thought that Oakland wasted $800 million on a BART connector to replace shuttle buses, but later projects are almost making that look like a bargain.

Too many make the mistake of believing the progressives when they say they want rail service to anywhere. They don’t really care if a single foot of track is ever laid down or not They only purpose of the rail projects is to siphon billions of dollars from taxpayers to well connected progressive companies and NGO’s. True in CA and LAX, and will be the same in Austin.

As they say history repeats itself. When SeaTac made it’s first renovation, it was more important to build parking garage adjacent to terminal then a light rail station. When light rail finally started is was projected so far over budget that federales were going pull funding. The City went back to taxpayers who swallowed and said ok. So, you can now take the light rail downtown to the airport painlessly(until you pay taxes on it).

Now, you can get on as far north as Lynwood(Everett planned). Also, you can go from UW to airport. And within the past year, you can go to and from Bellevue and Redmond(Microsoft hq). And that is a first by light rail over the Lake Washington floating bridge. A world’s first. So Gary, it only costs an unbelievable amount of taxpayer money.

#6166. Hyatt Hotel Promises Jonathan Adler Toiletries—But There’s Drugstore Shampoo On Its Housekeeping Cart

Hotel Avante in Mountain View, California advertises Jonathan Adler bath amenities. A reader photographed its housekeeping cart with a retail bottle of HASK shampoo resting among unbranded squeeze bottles. This is another JdV by Hyatt property, just a few miles from the Wild Palms hotel where I reported on DRIFT bulk toiletries on housekeeping carts while the guest bathroom bottles displayed Jonathan Adler branding. Apparently readers need to keep checking what’s on the carts. The brown bottle is HASK Tea Tree Oil & Rosemary Invigorating Shampoo, in the 12-ounce size. HASK is an affordable retail hair care brand, with products sold at CVS and other stores. Around it are condiment-style squeeze bottles. At least one has “Body wash” handwritten on tape. That identifies the type of product, without telling guests whose product it is. It seems like Hyatt a good reason to check what this hotel is using to refill its toiletries. But they had this reason at its sister property, too. There needs to be much stronger monitoring. Hyatt’s Hotel Avante page lists “Jonathan Adler bath amenities” across all six room categories. The hotel’s separate website promises that as well. I have no particular opinion on HASK shampoo. My issue is that a hotel should deliver the product they specifically advertise to guests. And if the bulk toiletries in the room say they’re a specific brand, they should be that brand. The reader describes Avante as Wild Palms’ sister property and they’re both part of the same ownership group. In November 2025, I published a reader’s photos from Wild Palms. The bathroom had Jonathan Adler bottles, while the housekeeping cart carried large jugs of DRIFT Hydrated Body Care. Then in January, Ben at One Mile at a Time published follow-up photos showing the bulk jugs with their labels removed. Wild Palms still advertises Jonathan Adler toiletries. I just wrote about the ketchup, mustard and mayonnaise bottle approach to hotel toiletries. Once the hotel keeps reusing the branded packaging, it can change the contents without changing anything the guest sees. An owner who substitutes a cheaper product keeps the savings, while Hyatt and the advertised toiletry company risk their reputations. Remind me again why bulk dispensers were a better idea than single use biodegradable packaging? I understand the dismay of false advertising but does anyone really pick a hotel based on the shampoo or soap offered vs loyalty points, location, free/discounted parking and breakfast, and location? I’m seriously interested.

@Ray: Pretty much any legitimate brand of shampoo would be acceptable to me, but I still don’t find it acceptable to advertise one brand and refill the bottles with a different brand.

If the shampoo bottles in the shower were labeled Suave, and we saw bulk bottles of Suave on the housekeepers’ carts (in the original packaging from Unilever, not bottles with handwritten labels on tape), that would give me more confidence with regard to the hotel’s shampoo policy than what this Hyatt is doing.

It wasn’t. I have some sympathy for the environmental argument for the re-usable bottles, but corporate culture in the US showing [again] that they will take advantage of anything they can to save a buck. The bulk bottles on the wall were never a good idea, if for no other reason than hygene (who thinks they replace these once a year, if at all). But this is another reason. Taking advantage of customers, even at ‘luxury’ properties. Makes me wonder if we overvalue hotels and should just go straight to Fairfield Inn.

And these are just the instances we know about. If there are confirmed sightings of this in the past couple of months, imagine the actual scope of the problem, I assume this is going on at thousands of hotels.

If I were at Jonathan Adler, I’d start off by suing Hyatt for false marketing (or legal equivalent). For us guests, seems like it’s time to start pushing legislation that will force compliance. Require unopened, personal-size bottles of toiletries in every room. I have no problem with requiring it to be biodegradable, but even without this, seems reasonable from a hygiene standpoint. Even anllowing accurately labeled [bulk] bottles might be a slippery slope – if hotels have openly flouted that by using ‘ketchup’ bottles to refill, I imagine their reaction to comply might be to buy a single bulk bottle of advertised brand for each cart, then keep refilling that with the cheap sub.

On the other hand, maybe hotels would just revolt and stop providing these toiletries as amenities. As a traveller, might be a PITA to bring my own, but preferable to what seems to be going on now.

It all comes out of the same large industrial drum in the basement labeled “Universal Cleaner Base – 200 L – Made in China.”

@Emcampbe and others: It was NEVER about the environment. Never. It was ALWAYS about thinking of a way they could market sh*t and get people to accept it — even praise them for it.

We’ve seen that very thing in comments on in these forums: Person A complains about this sort of con-job, and Person B comes back with, “Hey, at least they’re trying to save the planet.”

I fully agree with @Emcampbe that the first step should be for Adler to sue them, arguing Hyatt is knowingly damaging their brand by passing off inferior products as theirs. If the neighborhood Piggly Wiggly starting putting name brand labels on cheap generics it would be an easy lawsuit. This is no different.

Why would a libertarian law professor have a toiletry brand?

One real issue here is that I have allergies to some brands and if they were substituted in and I didn’t know, my skin might break out.

I agree that the switch isn’t a good look. I just feel like is no benefit in advertising a brand. Just list shampoo supplied.

Of the chains, Hyatt properties are the most egregious offenders of using condiment-style bottles to squeeze unknown products into dispensers that are never cleaned or sanitized. I’ve even seen this at Grand Hyatt properties.

I think it’s high time the elites are forced to use these low-quality products.

I’m not a shampoo snob, I don’t have enough hair to be one but this can cause some real problems for people with alleges.

Some are allergic/ sensitive to tea tree oil. I bring my own products because I don’t want to worry about a reaction away from home. Most will never have an issue.

@Ray Not the shampoo itself, but if a hotel quietly swaps what it advertises I’d wonder what else on the listing is loose. For the stuff you mention I compare the full stay, room plus parking and breakfast, not the headline rate. FWIW free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from a bunch of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory differ by country. Then let location decide

@Matt — You know what would solve this… better consumer protections… *wink*

@Maryland — Tried to mention to you earlier this week, I finally made it to western PA. Thank you again for recommending.

1990 great. Snow moving in any time. So many acres. So sad. I cry thinking about it

No one who travels likes the large bottles in the shower. Who knows what people put into them. I travel with my own soap etc. I don’t want any surprises.

@RT – I’ve known Jonathan for 30 years, and he never mentioned it to me! 😉

There are real working solutions already employed by other industries for this problem that keep operators honest while still allowing multi use containers. Welcome to the stage Heinz ketchup.

That company that figured it all out and have pretty successfully stopped every trick in the book by restaurants trying to get away with refilling Heinz bottles with cheaper crappier products.

They do things like: – Sell large multi use bottles to restaurants but do not allowing refilling in their contracts, they must be replaced. – they have created dispenser systems that can only be refilled by replacing internal sealed bags that cant be refilled (those big Heinz branded condiment boxes you use the pump handle to get ketchup out of). – They give restaurants Heinz bottles that are always transparent and the label has a red outline around the ages that is perfectly color matched with Heinz ketchup so is largely invisible when filled with Heinz ketchup but sticks out clearly when the bottle is full of a different brand’s ketchup. – And most of all they aggressively audit restaurants and sue if they find violations. – Probably way more tricks of the trade then that too.

The toiletry brands should employ some of the same techniques with hotels, they are not that hard. As long as the hotel is not lying about it and keeping them sanitized I actually like the user experience of larger multi use products as I like liquid soap better then bars and you don’t run out if your sharing a room with another person.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

The  is one of the most recognizable premium travel rewards cards on the market, offering everything from airport lounge access and hotel elite status to a long list of travel and lifestyle statement credits.

But with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), it's also a significant investment.

The Amex Platinum offers plenty of opportunities to offset that cost, especially if you travel frequently and can take advantage of its statement credits. However, many of its benefits come with restrictions, and getting the full value requires some effort.

So, who can actually get enough value from the Amex Platinum to justify its annual fee? Let's take a closer look at who should — and shouldn't — consider adding this card to their wallet.

For frequent travelers, airport lounge access is one of the biggest reasons to consider the .

The card offers access to one of the most extensive airport lounge networks available through a credit card, making it especially valuable if you spend a lot of time in airports.

Cardmembers can access American Express Centurion Lounges, receive a Priority Pass Select membership (enrollment required) and visit Delta Sky Clubs when flying on eligible same-day Delta flights. Delta Sky Club access is limited to 10 visits per year unless you spend $75,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year to unlock unlimited visits. Access is subject to eligibility requirements.

Amex also operates Centurion Lounges at more than 20 airports, so the benefit can be particularly valuable if you live near or frequently connect through an airport with one.

If you travel frequently and would otherwise pay for lounge access, the Platinum could help you save money while making your time at the airport more comfortable. And when combined with the card's other travel benefits and statement credits, lounge access can help make the $895 annual fee easier to justify.

While the is best known for its premium travel benefits, it also offers a growing list of lifestyle statement credits that can help offset its $895 annual fee.

For example, cardmembers can receive up to $400 in Resy statement credits each calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter) at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants* and up to $300 in Lululemon statement credits* (up to $75 quarterly) at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online.

The card also offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment statement credits* (up to $25 monthly) for eligible subscriptions, along with up to $120 annually toward an Uber One membership to fully cover an auto-renewing $96 annual or $9.99 monthly membership*.

If you're already spending money on dining, shopping and entertainment in these categories, the credits can provide meaningful value without requiring you to change your spending habits.

However, many of these benefits are divided into monthly or quarterly credits, so you'll need to keep track of when to use them. The Platinum is a particularly good fit for someone who doesn't mind managing these benefits and can consistently take advantage of them year-round.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum

The Amex Platinum can also be a valuable addition to your wallet if you regularly stay at Hilton, Marriott or luxury hotels.

Cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status, which can provide benefits such as bonus points on stays and potential room upgrades. You'll also receive Leaders Club Sterling status with The Leading Hotels of the World, a collection of independent luxury hotels. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Beyond elite status, one of the Platinum's most valuable hotel-related perks is its up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (up to $300 semiannually).

Cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits every six months on eligible prepaid bookings through American Express Travel®, including stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection properties, as well as select Airbnb Luxe stays.

The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe require a minimum two-night stay, and beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging credit.

Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with valuable benefits, including daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, room upgrades when available and a property credit valued at $100.

If you regularly book these types of stays, the lodging credit and additional perks can go a long way toward offsetting the card's annual fee. Just be sure to compare prices with booking directly, since rates through Amex Travel aren't always the lowest.

Related: How to maximize the Amex Platinum hotel statement credit

Chase's unofficial 5/24 rule generally makes applicants ineligible for many Chase cards if they've opened five or more personal credit cards across issuers within the past 24 months.

Travelers who are still eligible for Chase cards may want to prioritize products such as the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees) before exceeding that threshold.

If you've already built a collection of Chase rewards cards, the Amex Platinum could be worth considering as your next premium travel card.

The card also earns Membership Rewards points, giving you access to a separate collection of airline and hotel transfer partners that can complement an existing Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy.

Many people just starting in the points world underestimate the stringency of Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you're just getting started with travel rewards and remain under Chase's 5/24 threshold, you may want to think carefully before applying for the Amex Platinum.

Opening the card could count toward your 5/24 total and potentially limit your eligibility for Chase cards in the future. That could mean missing out on valuable welcome offers or benefits from cards you planned to open later.

However, once you get over 5/24, it may be hard to get back under, and there’s a massive opportunity cost in doing so. Having a plan and sticking to it will serve you well in the long term.

Of course, that doesn't mean everyone under 5/24 should avoid the Platinum. If its benefits are a particularly good fit for your travel habits, it may still make sense.

The provides 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or with American Express Travel (on up to $500,000 of spending each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

A card like the or (see rates and fees) may be a better fit because their broader travel earning categories can include eligible third-party airfare bookings.

The offers a long list of statement credits, but that doesn't necessarily mean every cardholder will get enough value from them to justify the $895 annual fee.

Following the card's 2025 refresh, several of its benefits are geared toward specific lifestyle purchases, including dining at Resy restaurants, shopping at Lululemon and purchasing an Oura Ring. (Cardmembers receive up to a $200 Oura Ring statement credit each calendar year. This statement credit applies to ring purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. Enrollment is required.)

Many of these credits also come with restrictions. For example, the Resy and Lululemon credits are distributed quarterly, meaning you'll need to use them throughout the year rather than all at once.

If you don't already spend money with these merchants, or you don't want to keep track of multiple credits and enrollment requirements, the Platinum may not be the best fit.

Before applying, carefully consider just how much these credits are worth to you; if they provide little to no value, another Amex card might be a better fit.

Related: 4 different flavors of Amex Platinum — which one is right for you?

Business owners with substantial expenses may find that is a better fit than the personal Platinum.

Although both cards carry an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), their earning rates and statement credits differ in ways that could make one more valuable than the other.

For example, the Business Platinum earns 2 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases in select business categories and on purchases of $5,000 or more, on up to $2 million in combined eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

The Business Platinum also provides up to $1,150 in statement credits per calendar year for U.S. Dell purchases: up to $150 each calendar year and an additional $1,000 statement credit after spending $5,000 on Dell purchases with the same card each calendar year (enrollment required).

You can also access the Pay with Points redemption option on the Business Platinum card, which gets you a 35% bonus for eligible flights with your selected airline using your Amex points (up to 1 million points back per calendar year). This is notably not available on the personal Amex Platinum.

These business-focused benefits may be more useful for someone with significant company expenses, while the personal Platinum may be a better fit for travelers who can maximize its lifestyle credits.

New cardmembers can find out their offer and may be eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus could be worth up to $3,500, which is nearly four times the card's $895 annual fee.

While this is the card's standard welcome offer, now could still be a good time to apply if you're eligible for an offer you're happy with and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases.

Just make sure you'll also get enough value from the card's ongoing benefits to justify its annual fee beyond the first year.

Related: The best time to apply for Amex cards based on offer history

The offers an impressive lineup of premium travel benefits and statement credits, but its $895 annual fee means it won't make sense for everyone.

For frequent travelers who value airport lounge access and luxury hotel perks, and can consistently use the card's lifestyle credits, there's plenty of potential to get more value than the annual fee.

On the other hand, travelers who prefer straightforward rewards or don't regularly use the card's benefits may find better value with a lower-annual-fee option.

Ultimately, the Platinum is worth considering if its benefits fit your existing spending and travel habits — not because of the total advertised value of its credits.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Amex Platinum.

#6163. Where Does the U.S.-Israel Relationship Go from Here?

Opposition to Israel now has a toehold in both parties.

Israeli and American flags are flown at the March for Israel rally on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., November 14, 2023.

In the days since the midterms, it has become clear that the U.S.-Israel relationship is under assault in both parties. On the left, a group of DSA-linked Democrats has been elected to Congress. Like their precursor Zohran Mamdani in New York City and led by Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, these new members place opposition to Israel at the center of their politics. It isn’t one concern among many but the defining issue of their candidacies. El-Sayed used his graceless and vengeful victory speech to attack Israel in barely disguised language: “Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here for schools here and health care here and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”

For the first time, both the Senate and the House will have — among the majority side — dedicated opponents of all aid to Israel, including even the sale of defensive weapons. They will see moves like an end to military assistance as weak half-measures, when much more must be demanded.

Israeli and American flags are flown at the March for Israel rally on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., November 14, 2023.

#6162. The Two Card Answer To Which Rewards Strategy Is Actually Best

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

When I talk to people about earning miles, it’s inescapable that the majority of miles are earned from rewards credit cards. Most people want to know simply, “what is the best credit card.” If pressed I do have an answer to that question, but the best answer is that it’s usually two different credit cards that you pair together, taking the best of each.

The first thing to understand about rewards cards is that, in addition to their basic features as a payments tool, bundled financing, and consumer protections, there are really three different ways a card adds value. You need to understand this to make sure you’re using yours in the right way.

Initial bonus. A card might offer 100,000 points as an acquisition bonus. That’s a great reason to get a card, but it isn’t a good reason to keep the card or to spend money on the card (once you’ve earned the bonus).

Benefits. You might get free checked bags or priority boarding, lounge access, for free Disney+. Those can be great reasons to have the card, and keep the card, but aren’t reasons to spend money on the card (outside of the spend on those activities, potentially).

Rebate on spend. The most rewarding card for the kind of spending you’re doing – that means earning the most points, and the most valuable points, that you can redeem for the rewards you value most. When people ask about the best card, they’re usually talking about the one that gives them the best return on their spending. Although if they value a card’s benefits, they need to be careful to keep that issue separate – get that card, sure, enjoy the benefits, but don’t just default to using it for spending, too. I think that the American Express Platinum Card® (see rates and fees) is great to have, it is incredibly valuable for its benefits, but my goodness do not actually spend money on that card outside of airline tickets. For spending the reason you want two cards is that you generally want (1) that earns the most points in the categories you spend the most, and (2) a card that earns more than one point per dollar on everything else. Don’t fall into the trap of getting a ‘grocery card’ and then earning just one point per dollar on everything else. You can frequently get two cards where the second one has no annual fee, even. Here are some of the very best pairings: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (See rates and fees) has an offer to earn 100k bonus points after you spend $8,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. What’s great is earning 3x (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases) on travel, shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, advertising purchases made with social media sites and search engines each account anniversary year. It has the same points transfer partners as Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees). And if you have some of the no annaul fee Chase cards, you can move the points from those cards over to Ink Business Preferred and then transfer them to airlines and hotel programs. And there are a number of Chase cards with no annual fee that earn points quickly, but on their own those points can’t be transferred to airlines or hotels. But if you earn points with one of those, you can transfer the points to your Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card and from there to miles and points in other programs. For instance, the Ink Business Cash card earns 5x on the first $25,000 in combined purchases at office stores and on internet, cable and phone services each account anniversary year. It earns 2x on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases at gas stations and restaurants each account anniversary year. Freedom Flex earns 3X on dining and at drugstores and 5x in rotating categories, on up to $1,500 spend each quarter. The Freedom Unlimited card earns 1.5x on all spend (but 3x on dining and at drugstores). I have multiple Freedom and Ink Business cards, personally. Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) has a $95 annual fee. It earns 3x on groceries, dining, gas stations and on EV charging as well as flights and hotels. That’s really strong. It’s offering 60,000 bonus ThankYou® Points after spending $4,000 in the first 3 months of account opening. And the points even transfer to American Airlines AAdvantage miles. oneworld: American Airlines AAdvantage, Cathay Pacific Asia Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer, Qatar Airways Privilege Club Star Alliance: Avianca LifeMiles, EVA Air Infinity MileageLands, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Thai Airways Royal Orchid Plus, Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles SkyTeam: Air France KLM Flying Blue, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Non-alliance: Emirates Skywards, Etihad Guest, JetBlue TrueBlue Hotels: Leading Hotels of the World Leaders Club, Accor ALL – Accor Live Limitless, Choice Hotels Choice Privileges, Preferred Hotels I Prefer, Wyndham Hotels Wyndham Rewards There’s also a $100 Annual Hotel Benefit. Once per calendar year, you receive $100 off a single hotel stay of $500 or more (excluding taxes and fees) when booked through CitiTravel.com, applied instantly at time of booking. You can supplement that strong earner with a Citi Double Cash card which earns 2x on everything and has no annual fee. If you were going to get just one card for your spending, set it and forget it, and didn’t want to juggle products then I think the single best heavy spending card has to be the Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees). It’s a $495 annual fee card. It earns the most points on most spending, and it earns the most valuable points. The only thing to flag is that there are some things, like tax payments, that it doesn’t earn points for. So if you’re relying on big quarterly tax deposits for your points-earning this isn’t the card for you. You can earn 50,000 Bilt Points after spending $4,000 on everyday purchases in the first 90 days + $300 of Bilt Cash. The card earns 2X points on everyday spend. Plus, you can use Bilt Cash to earn 3x on up to $25,000 in purchases, you get a $200 twice annual hotel credit (with a 2-night minimum stay), and earning the card’s 50,000 point bonus after $4,000 in non-housing spend in the first 3 months also gives you Gold status for a year and that lets you earn Bilt points through Rakutent at 1:1. You can earn 3.3 points per dollar when spending 75% of the amount of your rent or mortgage and then using Bilt Cash to earn points when paying through through Bilt, and then earn 3 points per dollar redeeming Bilt Cash for points accelerator. So the cap on earning 3 points or more is much higher than that. There’s actually a strategy to earn 4 points per dollar on all of your spending by foregoing Bilt Cash entirely. You can spend points at 1.25 cents apiece directly through their travel portal, and they have the best transfer partners (and biggest transfer bonuses). Star Alliance: Air Canada Aeroplan, Turkish Miles & Smiles, United Airlines MileagePlus, Avianca LifeMiles, TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go oneworld: Cathay Pacific Asia Miles, Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan, Iberia Plus, British Airways Club, Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Qatar Airways Privilege Club SkyTeam: Air France KLM Flying Blue, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Non-alliance: Emirates Skywards, Southwest Airlines, Aer Lingus Aer Club Hotels: World Of Hyatt, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, Hilton Honors, Accor ALL – Accor Live Limitless, Wyndham Rewards Still, I’m going to add 4x and 5x cards to my wallet. But the Bilt Palladium Card is also a great option as your ‘catch all card’ paired with the card that earns the biggest multiplier on your primary spend. The other major 2x everywhere card to consider is the Venture suite. For rates and fees of the American Express Platinum Card®, click here. You can supplement that strong earner with a Citi Double Cash card which earns 2x on everything and has no annual fee. If you were going to get just one card for your spending, set it and forget it, and didn’t want to juggle products then I think the single best heavy spending card has to be the Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees). It’s a $495 annual fee card. It earns the most points on most spending, and it earns the most valuable points. The only thing to flag is that there are some things, like tax payments, that it doesn’t earn points for. So if you’re relying on big quarterly tax deposits for your points-earning this isn’t the card for you. You can earn 50,000 Bilt Points after spending $4,000 on everyday purchases in the first 90 days + $300 of Bilt Cash. The card earns 2X points on everyday spend. Plus, you can use Bilt Cash to earn 3x on up to $25,000 in purchases, you get a $200 twice annual hotel credit (with a 2-night minimum stay), and earning the card’s 50,000 point bonus after $4,000 in non-housing spend in the first 3 months also gives you Gold status for a year and that lets you earn Bilt points through Rakutent at 1:1. You can earn 3.3 points per dollar when spending 75% of the amount of your rent or mortgage and then using Bilt Cash to earn points when paying through through Bilt, and then earn 3 points per dollar redeeming Bilt Cash for points accelerator. So the cap on earning 3 points or more is much higher than that. There’s actually a strategy to earn 4 points per dollar on all of your spending by foregoing Bilt Cash entirely. You can spend points at 1.25 cents apiece directly through their travel portal, and they have the best transfer partners (and biggest transfer bonuses). #6159. American Kept Charging A $75 Award Fee After No More Work Was Was Required, Former Loyalty Chief Says

American Airlines used to charge $75 to book an award ticket within 21 days of departure. Now the former head of AAdvantage says the airline kept collecting its expedite fee even after the process it was supposed to expedite became automated. Maya Leibman, who ran AAdvantage before becoming American’s Chief Information Officer, discussed this on the this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. The airline finally eliminated the fee in January 2020. Leibman was defending checked bag fees because there are people and equipment involved in moving bags. Then she offered an example of a fee she couldn’t defend. I think she’s wrong about bag fees based on cost of production (‘real cost fallacy’). Bags are charged as a form of price discrimination. Nonetheless, Leibman recalled the transition from a manual award process to online booking: “we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days.”

Maya Leibman, who ran AAdvantage before becoming American’s Chief Information Officer, discussed this on the this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. The airline finally eliminated the fee in January 2020.

Leibman was defending checked bag fees because there are people and equipment involved in moving bags. Then she offered an example of a fee she couldn’t defend. I think she’s wrong about bag fees based on cost of production (‘real cost fallacy’). Bags are charged as a form of price discrimination. Nonetheless, Leibman recalled the transition from a manual award process to online booking:

“we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days.”

The transaction, she pointed out, was “all done automatically.” The fee survived even though the narrative used to justify it was gone. The $75 close-in charge was waived for American’s elite frequent flyers.

American once tried to go further. In May 2008 they announced a $5 charge for booking award tickets on their website. The argument for telephone booking fees had been that agents cost money, and customers could avoid that charge by doing the work themselves online. Here American wanted to charge for the cheaper booking channel, too. I wrote about the announcement on May 30, 2008. Multiply millions of award redemptions by $5 and it was clearly a revenue opportunity since they were the monopoly redeemer of the currency. Members couldn’t take their AAdvantage miles and book travel somewhere else. Except the airline had already used the prospect of an award to persuade customers to earn those miles. Adding a charge when they tried to use them reduced the value of a reward they’d earned, and made it less likely they’d earn in the future. It left a bad taste in the customer’s mouth at exactly the moment they’re supposed to feel best about giving the airline business. As I wrote years ago, American never implemented that fee. They backed away without announcing the reversal. They took the criticism for imposing it and didn’t claim credit for listening to members. The Airline Had Already Been Paid To Give You Those Miles I don’t think airline prices have to track the cost of each transaction. Two passengers on the same flight, in the same cabin, pay different fares every day. Airlines price based on demand. There’s even an economic argument for charging more for last-minute awards: the airline might otherwise sell that seat for an expensive ticket, or the customer might otherwise pay cash for that expensive ticket. In the former case, revenue management is supposed to price the award so that’s not an issue. And neither case requires someone to hurry up and process an electronic ticket. Ultimately, eliminating a cash fee doesn’t even necessarily mean make awards cheaper. When American dropped its $75 charge, I pointed out that United and Delta had moved towards collecting more miles for close-in awards instead. That’s a bad trade for elites who used to have the cash fee waived but don’t get the extra mileage requirement waived. American stopped discounting awards to elites. I confess that there are times when I have, academically, mused about someone just walking behind the proverbial desk and changing a ticket (or something) in response to a fee.

Obviously there are all sorts of legal issues with that sort of thing, but the legal pleading would be amusing to read. “Blah Airlines charges a fee for a staff member to change a ticket. We are therefore suing John Doe for changing his own ticket. Because that’s bad.”

That was such an egregious fee because 1) it was fake, 2) they would release award availability close in, so then you had to pay the fee if you wanted access to the seats. #6155. Binoche Triumphs over Feminism

The great French actress Juliette Binoche can look at the world around her so naturally that no matter what character she’s playing (whether in Rendezvous, Flight of the Red Balloon, Summer Hours, Certified Cop, Camille Claudel 1915, Let the Sunshine In, Winter Boy, The Taste of Things, or in her Oscar-winning role in The English Patient), she presents a woman in a mode of inquiry.

In Queen at Sea, Binoche portrays middle-aged Amanda, a Frenchwoman living in England who is juggling a marital separation, a teenage daughter, a professorship, and her aged and senile mother, for whom she is responsible. Each aspect of troubled conscience contributes to Amanda/Binoche’s natural beauty. Binoche is a French version of the intelligence and sophistication associated with Irene Dunne in such films as The Awful Truth, Theodora Goes Wild, and Unfinished Business.

The considerable dramatic conflicts in Queen at Sea would be chaotic without Binoche to guide us through. As devised and directed by American filmmaker Lance Hammer, Queen at Sea catches the obstacles faced by Amanda and those closest to her. Starting with Amanda’s shock when she checks in on her senescent mother Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall) and stepfather Martin (Tom Courtenay), only to discover the seniors in flagrante delicto, Hammer’s method is both confrontational and complexly personal. Amanda reacts politically, calling in the state apparatus to resolve unexpected domestic issues. She’s alarmed by consensual sexuality that doesn’t meet her preference. “If we don’t get some help, it will overwhelm us,” she tells her stepfather, whose most eloquent response is to look at her with surprise, then steely anger.

Amanda interferes like the most aggravating Karen in contemporary cinema. But that’s precisely Hammer’s point and Binoche’s artistic venture. Queen at Sea brings to light the imperiousness of feminism that has seized contemporary Western life. Acting out of her own uncertainty, Amanda would be a dislikable pedant, except that she is steadfast and loving in her intentions toward her mother, her stepfather, and her daughter Sara (Florence Hunt) who, in Hammer’s balanced narrative contrast, is just beginning to discover her own sexual nature.

Queen at Sea is a schematic exercise from the first shot of the elderly Leslie and Martin slowly climbing up a public staircase. Everything is a negotiation with progress. That was also the problem with Hammer’s previous film, Ballast (2008), the condescending racial drama set in the American South. Since then, Hammer has been on an artistic sabbatical, teaching in academia until he made this second feature. Like Binoche, Hammer is also in a mode of inquiry, which comes through when Amanda, in professor-speak, belittles Martin’s intimacy with Leslie: “This disinhibition is a consequence of the disease eroding the areas of the brain used to keep the primal instincts in check.”

Martin responds rationally: “Why are you so keen to deprive her of something that gives her comfort, pleasure at a time in her life when she needs them most?” This is a genuinely difficult dilemma, such as few contemporary films have dared. Hammer achieves a level of respectable compassion, yet one can’t help longing for Mike Leigh to step in and rescue it all.

Queen at Sea raises an essential question: Must movies be variations on social issues, or personal experience? Hammer’s art-minded condescension was transparent in Ballast, but it’s more effective here in compositions that depict the emotional friction between Amanda and Sara through Mondrian squares and distance — the space observed on the retirement-home surveillance monitors that capture Leslie’s sexual abuse. Montages of Sara and her wild-haired friends exploring their sexuality pay homage to Brady Corbet’s The Brutalist. (The teens express their “fear of the sublime” while literally searching the world’s structure to find responsibility or freedom.) Through Amanda’s frustration, Lesley’s quiet, and Sara’s naïveté, Hammer probes the sexual intimacy that most feminist filmmakers don’t articulate. (Martin and the male experience are sidelined.)

That the politicization of cinema has been ruinous is apparent in how Queen at Sea improves on such age-themed films as of Away from Her, 45 Years, and Under the Skin. The empathic Hammer rejects the nihilism of Michael Haneke’s Amour, which Americans mistook for a geriatric love story. Inspired by an actress from the French tradition of sexual candor, an empath like Hammer can only provide a heroine who thinks her way past this era’s political clichés.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6153. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6150. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6147. AI Will Dehumanize the Job Hunt

I had been raised on stories of how the go-getters get going. You show up, you demonstrate desire to work, you list your skills and your aptitude, and someone out there, desperate for good, reliable help, will give you a chance. Bob Iger was a weatherman in Ithaca, then in 1974 started as a studio supervisor — a very low-level production job. He built a reputation for hard work and eventually became the CEO of Disney. Barry Diller started in the William Morris Agency mailroom. He got curious about how the entertainment business worked and used free time to read the agency’s files. He would eventually rise to higher positions, invent the “Movie of the Week,” and go on to run Paramount and Fox. Often these stories involve finding an older, experienced person as a mentor. Sol Price, the founder of FedMart, took Jim Sinegal under his wing. Sinegal had started at FedMart by unloading mattresses at 18. Sinegal rose through the company and co-founded Costco. We have tear-jerking movies about this, such as The Pursuit of Happyness.

All those stories highlight that market relations, careers, and success are not just a kind of abstract exchange and extraction of value, but really stories of human endeavor, development, and relationships. The market isn’t just the exchange of “utils,” money, and labor; at its best, it is a kind of theater for human virtue and adventure. Greed, grasping, or manipulation are sinful; hard work, creativity, and the courage to put yourself out there are our participation in the great good work of Providence.

Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

#6146. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.
